proposals.title: Abort a member-by-member enumeration after three negatives; ask the complement instead
proposals.trigger: Three or more consecutive questions that each test a single member of the same partition (one occupation, one country, one function class) have all come back negative.
procedure: Stop asking about further individual members of that partition.

Ask one grouped/complement question that covers the entire remaining block of that partition at once (e.g. 'none of the above kinds — is it in the remaining group?' phrased positively over the residual set).
If the grouped question returns yes, split the residual block roughly in half next, never one member at a time.
If the grouped question returns no, treat the partition itself as mis-framed: switch axis (origin, era, size, material, medium) rather than continuing inside it.
Never ask more than four member-level questions on any one axis in an episode.
successSignals: A yes arrives within one or two questions after the switch.
Each negative now eliminates a block rather than a single candidate.
failureSignals: Four or more negatives in a row on the same axis.
Turn count past half the cap with the entity's category still unresolved.
recovery: Re-read the yes answers only, restate the residual set out loud, and pick the next axis that splits it nearest to half.
invariants: No extra questions are spent; the grouped question replaces the member question that would have been asked.

proposals.title: Start naming concrete candidates once the residual set is small, not when forced
proposals.trigger: The accumulated yes answers already pin the entity to a recognizable narrow family (a nationality plus a profession, or a material plus a use class), or roughly two-thirds of the turn budget is gone.
procedure: Immediately list internally the 3-5 most probable concrete entities consistent with every yes and no so far.
If that list is non-empty, spend the next turn naming the single most probable one rather than asking another attribute question.
On a negative, do not return to broad attribute questions: ask one attribute that splits the remaining named candidates (age band, sub-genre, sub-type), then name the next candidate.
Keep at least three turns before the cap reserved for named guesses.
If no concrete name can be generated from the current yes set, that is the signal the last axis was too fine — ask one broad axis question, then re-attempt naming.
successSignals: A named guess is asked by roughly mid-episode and each later question is chosen to separate named candidates.
Episode ends on a bingo with turns to spare.
failureSignals: The answerer issues a forced-guess prompt before any candidate has been named.
Final turns contain the first and only named guesses.
recovery: On a forced-guess prompt, name the highest-prior candidate in the residual family rather than a hedged category phrase.
invariants: Named guesses consume the same turn an attribute question would have; the budget is reallocated, not increased.

proposals.title: Pivot axis immediately after each yes instead of refining the same axis
proposals.trigger: A question just returned yes, confirming a broad attribute, and the natural next question would subdivide that same attribute further.
procedure: After a yes, check whether the residual set is already small enough to name candidates; if so, name one.
Otherwise choose the next question on a different, independent axis (origin vs role vs era vs form) so the two constraints multiply rather than nest.
Only subdivide the just-confirmed attribute when no independent axis would split the residual set near half.
Re-evaluate after every yes; a yes is the cheapest moment to change direction.
successSignals: Yes answers accumulate across different axes and the candidate family shrinks fast.
Few than three questions are spent inside any single confirmed attribute.
failureSignals: Several questions in a row all drill into the branch opened by one yes while other axes stay unknown.
Many yes answers but still no concrete candidate in mind.
recovery: Write out which axes are still completely unconstrained and ask about the most discriminating one next.
invariants: Uses only evidence already received; no repeated or confirmatory questioning.
